title: Each of your eyes has a blind spot that your brain quietly fills in
body: At the back of each eye, the nerve fibres from the retina gather at the **optic disc** and leave as the optic nerve. There are no rods or cones on the disc, so the matching patch of each eye’s view is completely blind. You don’t normally notice, because the brain fills the gap from the surrounding detail and from the other eye, whose blind spot falls on a different part of the scene.

slides.alt: Animated diagram of an eye in cross-section: light focuses on the retina, its nerve fibres gather at the optic disc and leave as the optic nerve, and the disc has no light-sensing cells. Then a cross and a dot on a cream card for a blind spot test, with step-by-step instructions.

slides.heading: Where it sits
slides.text: In your view, each blind spot is about 12–15° to the outer side of where you look, and about 1.5° below it. The two eyes’ gaps fall on different parts of the scene, so with both eyes open, each eye helps fill in for the other.

slides.heading: Bigger than you’d think, in degrees of your view
slides.note: The full Moon looks about half a degree wide, so about 11 full moons fit across a blind spot.

slides.label: nerve fibres leave each eye through the optic disc
slides.text: They come from the retina’s ganglion cells. The disc is also where the retina’s main blood vessels come in and go out.

slides.heading: Whose eyes have no blind spot?
slides.explanation: Every animal with a backbone has a blind spot. Octopus eyes evolved separately: the optic nerve meets the light sensors from behind, so it never makes a gap in the retina.

slides.heading: Found in the 1660s
slides.text: The French scientist Edme Mariotte noticed the blind spot around 1668. People had assumed the place where the optic nerve meets the eye would be the most sensitive part of the retina; Mariotte showed it is blind. He presented it at the court of Louis XIV and to the Royal Society in London.

slides.question: Why can’t the optic disc see anything?
options: It has no rods or cones
The iris casts a shadow on it
Blood is too thick to see through
The lens can’t focus light there
slides.explanation: The disc is where the nerve fibres bundle together and leave the eye. There are no light-sensing cells on it, so light landing there is never detected.
